title: Chukat: look up (Numbers 21:4–9)
hookLine: looking at the copper serpent heals; the Mishnah says it was turning hearts toward heaven (Rosh Hashanah 3:8)

lines: HOW MUCH OF YOUR DAY IS LOOKING DOWN?
cards: How much of your day is spent looking down? At a phone, a keyboard, a sink full of dishes, the next step on the sidewalk. Your neck probably knows the answer.
The Torah has a story where looking up is the cure, quite literally. The people are walking the long way around the land of Edom. They're tired, they're sick of the manna, and they complain again.

teach.b: In paraphrase: fiery serpents bite the people, and many die. The people come to Moses and say, we've sinned; pray that the snakes go away. Moses prays.

And God doesn't remove the snakes. Instead: make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and in the words of the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "every one that is bitten, when he seeth it, shall live."
Moses makes a serpent of copper and raises it high, and whoever is bitten looks at it and lives.
In Hebrew there's a little echo: a nachash, a serpent, made of nechoshet, copper. The rabbis were uneasy. A metal snake that heals?
In the Mishnah, tractate Rosh Hashanah, they ask, in paraphrase: does a serpent kill, or a serpent bring life? No.

teach.h: WHEN THEY LOOKED UPWARD, THEY HEALED.
teach.b: When Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to their Father in heaven, they were healed; and if not, they wasted away. The object isn't the point. The looking up is.
The Mishnah says the same of Moses' raised hands in the battle with Amalek: the hands didn't win the war; the people looking up did. And the serpent had a second life.
It was kept, and the book of Kings says that in the days of King Hezekiah people were burning incense to it and calling it Nehushtan. Hezekiah smashed it to pieces.
The sign that once pointed upward had become something people stared at instead. Look up, the Mishnah says, not at the pole.

how: The copper serpent is read in the portion of Chukat, and the Mishnah's teaching about it, that healing came when Israel looked upward and turned their hearts to heaven, is often studied alongside it.

o: the portion where looking up at a copper serpent heals
a law about which snakes are clean to touch
a charm against snakes worn by desert travelers

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: God answered Moses' prayer by removing the snakes
the snakes stayed. Moses made a copper serpent, and whoever looked at it lived.
the Mishnah says the serpent itself had healing power
it says the people healed when they looked upward and turned their hearts to heaven.
the copper serpent was later destroyed by a king of Judah
Hezekiah smashed it because people were burning incense to it (2 Kings 18:4).

games.q: you're King Hezekiah. the copper serpent Moses made has been kept all this time, and people are burning incense to it. what do you do?
games.why: Hezekiah broke it in pieces. the sign that once pointed upward had become something people worshiped.

practice: Lift your eyes to the highest point you can see: the sky through a window, the top of a tree, or just the ceiling. Let your chin rise a little and your shoulders drop.
If you pray, turn your heart upward the way the Mishnah describes; if you don't, let your gaze rest somewhere higher than your worries.

wordCard.voice: Chukat. The portion where a copper serpent on a pole heals those who look up, and the Mishnah says it was the looking up that healed.

orig.note: Hebrew: a serpent of copper (Numbers 21:9), a play between nachash, serpent, and nechoshet, copper.

carryVoice: Your line: look up and live. It was never the copper that healed. Day four hundred sixty, done.

sources.q: every one that is bitten, when he seeth it, shall live.
